zmrig-os is a complete operating system that mines: a kernel, a small initramfs and a read-only Alpine root filesystem containing zmrig and almost nothing else. Write it to a USB stick, boot the rig, type your wallet, and it is mining. Nothing has to be installed and nothing on the machine is modified. If you would rather not depend on the stick, the same image installs onto the machine's own disk with one command, and from then on it looks after itself: zmrig-os install --disk /dev/nvme0n1 # partition, copy, boot from the disk Install to disk and Updates below are the whole story; the rest of this page is what the image does and how to change it. # grab the image for your CPU from the releases page, then sudo dd if=zmrig-os-<version>-x86-64-v3.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync Two builds are published. x86-64-v3 needs AVX2 (any x86 CPU since roughly 2015) and is the default; x86-64-v2 runs on everything since Nehalem. The image is compiled for one level and the updater never offers the other one.

GRUB appears; the default entry is max hashrate. The console shows the ZMRIG banner and asks for your Monero address. Paste it, press Enter, and the hashrate line starts within a few seconds. The address is checked before it is used: 95 or 106 characters, base58 alphabet, starting with 4 or 8. A wallet typed with a 0 or an l — the two characters base58 drops precisely because they are misread — is refused instead of mining to nowhere.

A rig with no keyboard is configured from the kernel command line. Press e on the GRUB entry, or edit grub.cfg on a fleet image: zmrig.os.wallet=4... zmrig.os.pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 zmrig.os.worker=rig-07 zmrig.os.mode=max zmrig.os.maxtemp=70 zmrig.os.maxtemp is the temperature limit for safe mode and for any mode that arms the governor. The wizard does not appear when a wallet is already known. zmrig.os.nostart=1 boots the machine without mining, which is what a repair stick wants.

The miner's aggressiveness is a single word, changeable while it runs: zmrig-os mode eco # restart with half the cores and the watt profile zmrig-os mode safe 70 # ... and never let the CPU past 70 C zmrig-os status # what is hashing, at what rate, at what temperature Mode Threads Priority Profile Huge pages For max cache-aware, all cores 5 free reserved at boot the default balanced cores − 1 on 4+ cores 3 free reserved at boot a rig you also log into eco half the cores 1 watt THP madvise quiet and cool safe cores − 1 on 4+ cores 19 (nice) watt reserved at boot a machine that must not break light all cores, 256 MiB cache 2 free none under 2.5 GiB of RAM There are GRUB entries for each one, so a machine with no network and no keyboard can still be changed: the mode travels on the kernel command line and is applied at boot.

safe is the only mode that treats the machine's temperature as a limit rather than a side effect. It leaves one core for the OS and the fan controller, drops to the lowest scheduling priority there is, never writes the MSR registers, and arms the miner's thermal governor at 72 °C (change it with zmrig-os mode safe 68): zmrig-os status mode safe (max 72 C) thermal 64 C The governor runs once a second on the miner's own monitor thread. At 72 °C it parks one thread (at most every 30 s), at 80 °C it parks one immediately (at most every 5 s), at 87 °C it stops hashing altogether, and it comes back down the ladder — one thread at a time, two minutes of cool per step — as the box cools. Nothing is rebuilt on the way: a parked thread keeps its VM, the dataset stays in RAM and the pool connection stays open, so a hot afternoon costs the shares it did not compute and nothing else. It reads only CPU sensors (coretemp, k10temp, zenpower, cpu_thermal, acpitz, Super I/O), so a warm NVMe never costs a thread. On a machine with no sensor at all it says so once and keeps the thread count it was given. For a laptop, a shared office box, or any rig whose owner would notice it breaking, this is the mode to run. It gives up a few percent of peak hashrate at 20 °C and it does not spend the hot hours hardware-throttled at a rate it cannot control.

The live stick is deliberately disposable: /etc/zmrig lives in RAM and a reboot forgets it. An installed rig is the other half of that trade. zmrig-os install --disk /dev/nvme0n1 --dry-run # what would happen zmrig-os install --disk /dev/nvme0n1 # do it The disk is repartitioned, not shared: Partition Size Contents BIOS boot 1 MiB core.img, for a machine that boots in BIOS mode EFI 100 MiB BOOTX64.EFI, for UEFI root the rest kernel, initramfs, rootfs-a.squashfs, config Then it copies, verifies what it wrote (by reading the new filesystem back and hashing the squashfs), and prints remove the stick and boot from the disk. There is no bootloader package on the machine: the two GRUB images are built when the ISO is built and travel inside it, so the install needs no network and no grub-install. Everything after that is automatic: the miner starts, the config persists, the thread count is measured on the machine it will run on, and the daily update job is already enabled.

Add one parameter to the boot entry and walk away: zmrig.os.install=/dev/nvme0n1 The machine installs, reboots into its own disk and starts mining. With Ventoy that is: pick the ISO, press e, add the parameter. A fleet is the same parameter on every machine with the disk name that model uses.

An installed rig checks once a day, from busybox crond (/etc/periodic/daily), so there is no extra systemd timer and no package to keep. zmrig-os auto --check # is there anything newer? zmrig-os auto --apply # do it now instead of at 03:00 The miner is written next to the running system, not into /usr/local/bin — that directory is RAM, so an update there would last until the reboot. The previous binary is kept, and the miner is restarted into the new one. The OS image (AUTO_IMAGE=1, off by default) is written into the other slot, verified, and only then made the default for the next boot. An update that will not boot undoes itself. The initramfs counts boots that never became a mining rig; three of them flip the machine to the other slot and reboot. zmrig-os slot shows both, zmrig-os slot b picks one. AUTO_UPDATE=0 turns the whole thing off. No manifest reachable means "offline", which is not an error: the rig keeps mining and the job exits 0.

The harshest part of RandomX is memory, and the operating system decides almost all of it. On a general-purpose install every setting below is a fight against a package upgrade or a systemd unit. Here they are the defaults: It is 158 MB, and the number is a build output. The stock Alpine initramfs (171 MB, never read — the image builds its own), the GPU/Wi-Fi/switch firmware (660 MB → 16 MB) and the sound, video-capture, GPU, InfiniBand, ISDN, WAN, CAN, IIO, NFC, Bluetooth and staging drivers are not in it. Every build writes dist/size-report.txt with the biggest directories, the biggest files and the totals, so "why is the image this big" has an answer with numbers in it. Before this the same image was 1081 MB. --firmware all puts the firmware back for a board with a NIC outside the keep list. 2 MiB pages are reserved by the initramfs, before any userspace program has fragmented memory. That is the +4–6 % on top of transparent huge pages, and it is the one tuning step that is nearly impossible to do later in the day. Transparent huge pages stay enabled (always on the max entries). Turning them off costs about 28 % — measured, see Performance. The CPU governor is performance, set by the same step that reserves memory, before the miner starts. swappiness=1, so the 2.3 GiB dataset is never paged out; write-back throttled so a log rotation cannot stall a mining thread; 64 MiB kept free so a burst allocation does not trigger reclaim mid-hash; zone_reclaim_mode=0 so a multi-socket box does not stall on one node; NMI watchdog off, because nothing has ever been detected by it on a mining rig. Nothing else runs. No desktop, no update daemon, no telemetry. OpenRC, sshd, chrony and the miner. The binary is static (musl, one 19 MB file with no libc dependency), so an image update cannot break it and it runs on any distribution you copy it to.

documents.t: Long uptime is not one feature, it is a chain of them: the miner exits on a stall or on a run of rejected shares (--health-restart, 900 s), and says so in the log; zmrig-os run restarts it 10 s later, forever; five failed starts in a row reboot the machine, because at that point the operating system is the thing that is broken; logs rotate at 8 MB, so a notebook that has been mining for a year still boots; chrony keeps the clock right, because a pool login over TLS fails on skew. zmrig-os doctor prints every check the boot makes, with the value it found: PASS binary zmrig 6.36.0 - ZMRIG by @nggkhaiz PASS wallet 46SQLW7D...ysb5tJ PASS memory 32044 MB total, need 2400 MB PASS hugepages 1168 x 2 MB reserved PASS thp always PASS governor performance WARN msr not applied (VM, or no msr module) PASS swap off PASS dns gulf.moneroocean.stream resolves PASS config miner --check passed

Thread count is the one number that differs per box, and the cache heuristic assumes 2 MiB of L3 per thread. Let the machine answer instead: zmrig-os autotune 8 # 8 s per candidate, winning count pinned in the config The result is written to os.conf; THREADS="auto" returns to the heuristic. It tunes the machine first — huge pages, THP, governor — because measuring an untuned box answers the wrong question. It also happens on its own. On a rig that has never been measured, the miner starts immediately and, ninety seconds later, the supervisor measures the machine while it mines. The answer is written to the config and the miner reloads once. No idle boot, no reboot, and the reload is not counted as a crash. AUTO_AUTOTUNE=0 turns it off, and a thread count you set by hand is never overwritten: threads auto (the machine is being measured) threads 8

A measurement is a claim about the future, and a machine only sometimes keeps it: a dust-filled heat sink, a stick of RAM that started erroring, a background job left running. None of that announces itself, and all of it looks the same — a hashrate under the rate this box measured. The image therefore stores the result next to the thread count (MEASURED_HS, MEASURED_THREADS, TUNED_AT) and compares the two every fifteen minutes: measured 1234 H/s at 4 thread(s), 6 h ago The rule is conservative, because a needless re-measure costs more than the drift it chases: Condition Why the 15-minute rate, not the 10-second one a dataset build or a pool reconnect moves the short window below 75 % of the measured rate a rig at 90 % is having a normal day at least 250 H/s measured on a small rig two runs differ by tens of percent at least 6 h since the last measurement a re-measure runs at the wrong count for ~90 s still the count the measurement chose a number set by hand is never revisited When all five hold, the rig says what it saw and measures again. zmrig-os doctor reports the same comparison on demand.

documents.t: base Alpine Linux latest-stable — 3.22.x today — musl, OpenRC kernel linux-lts (linux-virt for a VM) root filesystem squashfs, zstd level 19, 1 MiB blocks, read-only initramfs busybox + ~30 modules, zstd when the kernel's config says it can unpack it, gzip otherwise boot GRUB, BIOS and UEFI, both built with the image The image writes that table to /etc/zmrig/base, and zmrig-os version prints it, so a bug report carries its own base. ./os/upstream.sh prints the same from the source, and --check answers whether a rebuild would change anything — the Alpine mirror serves latest-stable, so the weekly build compares it with the alpine field of the last published manifest instead of rebuilding to be sure.

On an installed disk this is unnecessary: the config is on the boot medium and comes back by itself. On a live stick the root filesystem is read-only, so the config lives in RAM and disappears at reboot; a small partition fixes that: zmrig-os persist /dev/sdb1 # format, label ZMRIGDATA, copy the config The initramfs finds it by label on every boot and copies os.conf and /root/.ssh/authorized_keys in.

The image has no web UI on purpose — a web app is another thing to patch. What it has is the miner's own JSON API, off by default: API_PORT="18080" API_HOST="0.0.0.0" API_TOKEN="a long random string" With those three lines, http://rig:18080/2/summary answers anyone holding the token, which is what a fleet dashboard, Home Assistant or a curl in a cron job needs. Leaving API_HOST at 127.0.0.1 keeps it on the machine.

A machine that boots a hundred rigs should not need a keyboard on each of them. zmrig-os fleet --url https://your-fleet (or zmrig.os.fleet= on the kernel command line) points a rig at a Telegram and Discord bot, and zmrig-os id prints the Device ID you enrol it with. Wallets, pools, coins, modes and updates are then set from the chat, and a rig that goes quiet tells you. Telegram and Discord control is the guide.

documents.t: The automatic job above uses the same commands; these are the manual versions: zmrig-os update --check # what is published for this channel zmrig-os update --apply # 19 MB binary, sha256 verified, swapped in zmrig-os update --iso --write /dev/sdb1 # flash a newer image to another stick On a live stick --apply patches the running image and is lost on reboot — reboot and you are back on the version that was burned in. That is the whole rollback procedure and it needs no menu. On an installed rig it lands on the boot medium and survives. --iso refuses to write the device the machine booted from. Channels: stable follows master releases, beta follows the rolling pre-release under the os-beta tag. Both publish a manifest per instruction level, which is what the updater reads — and the two are in different places, because releases/latest never points at a pre-release: stable https://github.com/MoLik-Labs/ZMRIG/releases/latest/download/zmrig-os-stable-x86-64-v3.json beta https://github.com/MoLik-Labs/ZMRIG/releases/download/os-beta/zmrig-os-beta-x86-64-v3.json

The console is an autologin root shell — the wizard needs it, and physical access to a rig is already root. Everything below exists because that is true. SSH is key-only: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password, no passwords, no keyboard-interactive. zmrig-os ssh-key add then rc-service sshd start. No package manager runs at runtime: the image is what was built. Updates are sha256-verified before the binary is moved into place; a mismatch fails and leaves the old file alone. Nothing phones home. The only outbound traffic is your pool, NTP and, if you ask for it, an update check.

sudo ./os/deps.sh # xorriso, mtools, grub, squashfs-tools, qemu sudo ./os/build-iso.sh # → os/out/zmrig-os-<version>-x86-64-v3.iso sudo ./os/build-iso.sh --smoke # build, then boot it in QEMU and read the log The image is rebuilt by CI whenever os/, zmrig/ or scripts/tune-linux.sh change, and every release keeps its ISO. The workflow also runs on pull requests that touch os/, so a broken image fails before it is merged. The build also publishes the manifest zmrig-os update consumes, so an image in the field can move forward without being rewritten. Five steps, and every one of them is a build step rather than a person remembering: a push builds and boots both architectures in QEMU; master publishes v<version> and BETA publishes the rolling os-beta, replacing assets in place so a version's link never rots; a Monday run asks os/upstream.sh --check whether Alpine moved and skips the build if it did not; the job then fetches every asset over HTTPS and rewrites the notes with the links; and each rig's daily job applies the miner, or the whole image into the spare A/B slot with AUTO_IMAGE=1.

Not a GPU miner. Not an overclocking tool — memory timings and voltage belong to firmware. Not a way to make MSR writes work inside a virtual machine: the hypervisor rejects them and the miner stays on the portable path, which zmrig-os doctor reports instead of hiding.

GitHub Pages serves this documentation and GitHub serves the images, so nothing here is required. serve/ exists because three things are nicer on your own host: a link that does not change when a version does, a download page that always lists the current asset with its checksum, and a site that works where GitHub Pages is blocked or slow. One Node process, no dependencies, no build step of its own. cd site && npm install && npm run build && cd .. cd serve && cp .env.example .env && npm start # http://localhost:8080 Every setting has a default, so .env.example is a reference rather than a requirement; it lists the port, the site root, the repository the releases come from, how long the feed is cached, and the public URL that /download prints.

That is the whole point: a script, a Ventoy menu or a sticky note can name the same URL for a year.

render.yaml is a blueprint with two services — the pool and this host. The deploy button reads the same file; New → Blueprint and picking the repository does the same thing. Render: builds the documentation with SITE_BASE_URL=/, because this host serves from the root of its own domain rather than from /ZMRIG/; writes the precompressed copies once, at deploy time; starts node serve/server.js. Nothing in it is a secret. The GitHub API is read anonymously and the feed is cached for ten minutes — 60 calls an hour at most, well inside the limit. A free instance sleeps after fifteen minutes without traffic and wakes on the next request in about a second. If that is not good enough, point any free uptime monitor at /healthz every five minutes.

Everything the site serves is read into memory once, at boot: 238 routes, 6.31 MB raw, 1.63 MB compressed. After that a request is a Map lookup and one end(). no stat, no open, no readdir per request; Brotli and gzip written once at deploy (or at boot when a sidecar is missing); ETag on every response, and a conditional request is answered with 304 before the body is touched; fingerprinted assets are immutable for a year, HTML revalidates; one connection stays open for 65 seconds, so a page and its assets share it; the release feed is fetched once per ten minutes, not once per visit; a compressed copy older than the page it belongs to is ignored, so a stale sidecar from an earlier build cannot pin the site to last week's content. The two pages this process renders itself (/download and the JSON feed) carry Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none' — one HTML file, no script at all. Measured here (2 vCPU, keep-alive, warm): / at 0.25 ms p50 and 0.81 ms p95, /docs/intro at 0.19 ms, an asset at 0.35 ms, eight concurrent requests at 0.89 ms p50. Brotli takes the home page from 16 KB to 3.9 KB. A Render instance has different CPU and a real network in front of it; nothing here has been measured there.

The feed keeps the last good answer and the page says so — and says what to fix (name lookup failed, timed out, TLS certificate rejected) rather than Node's fetch failed. If GitHub has never answered since the process started, the page says that too and the links it has still work, and /iso/* answers 404 instead of redirecting into nothing. Nothing 500s because a third party is unavailable.

cd serve && npm test # 45 checks File table, negotiation, 304, traversal attempts, escaping of everything that comes from GitHub — including a javascript: URL in a release asset — the three redirects, a failing feed that explains itself, a stale precompressed sidecar, q=0 in Accept-Encoding, the policy on the pages this process renders, and the real process booting and stopping on a socket. The full operator notes — every environment variable, the cache lifetimes and how to tune them — are in doc/WEB.md.

The miner re-reads the profile at startup, so unplugging and restarting the service is enough to switch.

--max-temp is the one number this mode is built around. It arms a governor that runs once a second, reads the hottest CPU sensor and gives back threads as the box warms: sudo zmrig -o gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --max-temp=72 --profile watt what happens when nothing below 72 °C one thread is parked at 72 °C, at most once every 30 s a thread is parked immediately at 80 °C (target + 8), at most once every 5 s hashing stops at 87 °C (target + 15) even on one thread hashing resumes at one thread once the sensor is back under 65 °C a thread comes back after two minutes below 67 °C (target − 5) The two speeds matter. At the target a spike is normal — a boost bin, one burst of shares — so it waits. At the hard cap the hardware is already protecting itself, so it acts at once. Stepping back up is deliberately slow: cooling for two minutes and heating up in ten seconds is how a fan bearing dies, and it also makes the measured average worse than holding one thread less. Nothing is rebuilt while this happens. A parked thread keeps its VM and the dataset stays in RAM, so a pause costs the shares it did not compute and nothing else — the pool connection stays open. thermal: holding 72 C max - k10temp/Tctl reads 61.5 C now; 8 thread(s), step down at 72 C, pause above 87 C thermal: 73.4 C on k10temp/Tctl -> 7 of 8 threads (target 72 C; 1 step-down(s), 0 step-up(s) so far) thermal: 81.2 C on k10temp/Tctl -> 6 of 8 threads (target 72 C; 2 step-down(s), 0 step-up(s) so far) zmrig --check prints whether a governor is armed and what it can see, which is the difference between "it throttled" and "it has no sensor and never could": thermal hold 72 C: k10temp/Tctl 61.5 C now, step down at 72 C, pause above 87 C (--no-thermal turns it off) thermal off (no --max-temp: nothing throttles, however hot the box gets) The sensors are the CPU ones only — coretemp, k10temp, zenpower, cpu_thermal, acpitz and the Super I/O chips — so a warm NVMe or a warm GPU never costs a thread. A machine with no sensor at all says so once and keeps mining at the thread count it was given: an unreadable thermometer is not a reason to stop earning. --thermal-file=PATH points the governor at a file instead, for a board whose sensor is exposed by the BMC.

documents.t: The default is L3 cache / 2 MiB, capped at the logical CPU count. On a 2 vCPU VPS with 54 MB of L3 that is two threads, which is also the best measured value: 814 H/s with two, 408 H/s with one. zmrig --autotune=8 # no pool required, 8 s per candidate threads hashrate verdict 1 499.625 H/s best so far 2 999.750 H/s best so far best: 2 thread(s) at 999.750 H/s autotune-best-threads=2 A difference under 2 % counts as noise, so it does not change the thread count because of one lucky run.

sudo zmrig -c /etc/zmrig/config.json --check config ok pool wss://my-relay.example.com:443/pool user=4Ad algo=auto (all RandomX variants) route connect 10.0.0.7:443, Host: my-relay.example.com proxy socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 threads 2 (default would be 2) cpus [0,1] on 2 cpu(s), 2 physical core(s) mode auto, huge pages on, jit on memory rx/0 maps 2336 MB, 1168 pages of 2 MiB: no pages reserved; transparent huge pages collapse the mapping instead thp madvise (default): the hint this miner sets is honoured, so no root step is needed msr intel preset; reading /dev/cpu/0/msr needs root (off: --msr is worth 5-15% on Zen 3/4 …) The memory line is the coin's own size — panthera maps 192 MB, 96 pages — and the thp line answers the question it raises: madvise and always mean the kernel backs the mapping with 2 MiB pages without any root step, never means it does not and the miner will be ~28 % slower until pages are reserved. --check reads the file and prints; it opens no socket and allocates no dataset. If the file is root-only, run it with sudo or you get cannot read …: check the path or run as root.

Precedence, highest first: command-line flags the file passed with -c/--config the miner's defaults Only flags you actually type override the file. zmrig -c config.json --verbose does not lose "mode": "light" or "huge-pages": false. (Before 6.26.0-mo9 it did; see the changelog.)

sudo systemctl stop zmrig sudo cp /etc/zmrig/config.json /etc/zmrig/config.json.bak sudo -e /etc/zmrig/config.json zmrig --check -c /etc/zmrig/config.json # parse and validate, do not mine sudo systemctl start zmrig --check exits non-zero and prints the offending key, which is faster than reading the journal after the service has already restarted four times. Autosave "autosave": true lets the miner rewrite the file when it changes something it owns (a tuned thread count, for example). If you want a file the miner never touches, set it to false and restart rather than editing a running config.

This tree ships three interchangeable mining engines behind one installer, one config file and one HTTP API: Engine Path Language Why it exists zmrig zmrig/ Zig the default: single binary, no runtime dependencies, same RandomX code xmrig src/ C++ the reference build, GPL-3.0, the widest algorithm and hardware coverage proxy proxy/ Node.js the farm front end; no hashing, only routing /etc/zmrig/engine records which one the installer chose, so every later oneclick.sh command acts on the same engine without being told again.

zmrig/src/ ├── main.zig startup, signals, the mining loop, report writing ├── options.zig the CLI surface, config-file parsing and validation ├── stratum.zig login, job parsing, share submission, refusals, cooldown ├── transport.zig TCP, TLS, WebSocket, SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, DNS ├── job.zig blob assembly, extranonce handling, target comparison ├── miner.zig thread pool, nonce spacing, hashrate windows, share accounting ├── api.zig JSON documents for the HTTP API ├── api_http.zig the HTTP server itself ├── report.zig ZMRIG1. report codes ├── health.zig the watchdog state machine ├── hugepages.zig reservation and verification of 2 MiB pages ├── topology.zig core detection, cache sharing, thread placement ├── autotune.zig picks thread count and affinity for the host ├── verify.zig share re-hashing for pool operators ├── log.zig the log format, levels and timestamps └── util.zig base64, hex, time, small helpers Nothing is linked beyond libc. There is no allocator in the hash loop, no background GC, and no dependency that could change behaviour between builds.

Parse flags, then config.json, then the engine marker — in that order, so a flag on the command line always wins. Detect the CPU: cores, SMT siblings, L3 size, NUMA nodes. Reserve huge pages; if the reservation fails, log the exact command that would fix it and continue rather than refusing to start. Build the RandomX cache (256 MiB) and, in fast mode, the dataset (2 GiB). This is the 15–25 s startup cost; light mode skips the dataset. Start the worker threads with the affinity chosen by autotune.zig. Open the stratum connection: DNS, transport, login, first job. Start the HTTP API (default 127.0.0.1:18080) and, if requested, the report file writer.

A job arrives as a 76-byte blob with a target. The miner writes the nonce into bytes 39–43, hashes, compares the result against the target, and on a hit sends submit upstream. Nothing on that path allocates, and nothing takes a lock: each thread owns a contiguous slice of the 32-bit nonce space, and its position is advanced by a stride chosen so two threads never collide. The scratchpad lives in huge pages for the whole run. That is the difference between 814 H/s and 634 H/s on the reference machine — see Benchmarks.

proxy/src/ is a small pipeline: server.js accepts rig connections, downstream.js models each rig, extranonce.js assigns prefixes, vardiff.js sets difficulty per rig, target.js compares hashes, upstream.js holds the single pool connection, tunnel.js handles WireGuard/Tailscale/ Cloudflare, and access.js enforces CIDR and token rules. blob.js is the only place that knows the layout of a Monero job — read that first.

pool/src/ accepts shares, re-hashes each one with zmrig --verify-share, keeps PPLNS weights as difficulty × time, and writes every block to audit.jsonl. Payouts go out through monero-wallet-rpc. pool/worker/ is a Cloudflare Worker that bridges WebSocket to TCP so the pool can run on a platform that only speaks HTTP.

Question File Why did a connection fail? zmrig/src/stratum.zig, zmrig/src/transport.zig Why this thread count? zmrig/src/autotune.zig, zmrig/src/topology.zig Why is hashrate low? zmrig/src/miner.zig, zmrig/src/hugepages.zig What does this API field mean? zmrig/src/api.zig Why did the service restart? zmrig/src/health.zig Why is a rig not being paid? pool/src/, then audit.jsonl Why is a rig not submitting? proxy/src/vardiff.js, proxy/src/target.js The longer C++ map — every directory in src/, the thread inventory and the RandomX pipeline — is in doc/ARCHITECTURE.md.
Every suite here runs without a real pool, and no suite needs a wallet.

./zmrig/out/zmrig --self-test # full: needs 2 GiB of RAM ./zmrig/out/zmrig --self-test=light # skips the dataset checks ./zmrig/tests/run.sh # self-test plus the API checks --self-test checks the reference rx/0 vectors, pipelined hashing, and that a dataset built from the cache produces the same result as a full-memory build. oneclick.sh verify calls it before it checks the fee.

zmrig/tests/health.sh runs the miner against a fake pool twice, to prove both directions: Case Expected A well-behaved pool health stays ok, nothing is logged as an error, no restart A pool rejecting every share health becomes rejected, the process exits code 3 so systemd restarts it, and the log says how to disable that Plus seven unit tests for the state machine (health.zig): a pause is not an error, one or two stale shares are normal, and a dip has to last before it counts as degraded.

It starts a fake pool, a TLS shim, HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies and a WebSocket server on the local machine, then makes the miner talk to all of them: ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --quick # 10 s per case ./zmrig/tests/net.sh # 18 s per case ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --soak # adds a 4-minute soak ./zmrig/tests/net.sh --only api,tcp Group Case What it proves Transport tcp, tls, ws, wss login, job, share submission ws path the server receives /miner wss via socks5 WebSocket over TLS through SOCKS5 CDN cloudflare wss on 443 with the right Host header Proxy http proxy, socks5 proxy CONNECT and auth reach the right target API http api, http api token, http api 404 summaries, token enforcement, unknown paths Failure login rejected, idle watchdog, pool failover the error is visible; reconnect and failover work hostile pool garbage input does not stop shares from being submitted Seed seed change four dataset rebuilds, mining continues Soak soak 4 minutes of seed changes, algorithm changes and a dropped link A full run takes 12–15 minutes on 2 vCPU, because each case has to produce a share and the suite runs in --mode light (50–70 H/s). A last run on that machine: 29 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped Per-case logs land in /tmp/zmrig-net.XXXXXX/, printed at the end. When a case fails, read that case's log first (cloudflare.log, shim-cf.log, pool.log).

Ports. The suite uses 4800 for the pool and 4801–4813 for shims. A leftover process holding 4800 makes the cloudflare case fail with accepted=0 while the miner log says login ok. The script kills strays and refuses to start if something else owns the port. CPU load. Do not run benchmarks in parallel — you get either an OOM kill or a corrupted measurement. Huge pages. light mode means no 2 GiB reservation is needed; 50–70 H/s is expected, not a regression.

sudo ./oneclick.sh verify With the Zig engine it runs the self-test and then scripts/verify-fee.sh, which reads the rate, the wallet and the --donate-level=0 off switch out of the binary and fails if a second address or an upstream donation endpoint appears. With the C++ engine it runs scripts/verify-fee-free.sh, which additionally checks that the binary prints DONATE 0% when handed --donate-level=9. The check greps for endpoints and addresses, not for the word donate: the monitoring API legitimately returns "donate_level": 0, and a naive grep raises a false alarm. That has happened here, and it was fixed.

./zmrig/tests/cli.sh # flag parsing, help text, exit codes ./zmrig/tests/unit.sh # unit tests across the Zig modules node --test pool/tests/*.test.js bash tests/oneclick/plan.sh && bash tests/oneclick/config.sh && bash tests/oneclick/governor.sh plan.sh is the one that matters most after a change to the installer: it asserts the exact command a user would copy for a dozen flag combinations.

cd site && npm test # unit tests for the calculators and the command builder cd site && npm run build # fails on a broken internal link or a bad component The link check is the point of npm run build: onBrokenLinks and onBrokenMarkdownLinks are both set to throw, so a renamed page cannot ship as a 404.

The network suite uses its own ports and a fake pool, so it does not touch the real miner. But if the real miner holds the huge pages, the full --self-test may not have enough RAM for its dataset — use --self-test=light, or sudo ./oneclick.sh stop first.

XMR/day = (hashrate / 1000) × xmr_per_khs_day This is the honest number for a switching pool such as MoneroOcean, because the algorithm switching is already inside the pool's rate. From network hashrate. The calculator adds a system overhead (25 W by default) and divides by PSU efficiency (87 %) because the number inside a report code is CPU package power: it excludes the mainboard, disks, fans and the losses of the PSU. Three levels of accuracy: A meter at the wall — the only exact one. Read the watts and either type them into the power column or pass --power W; a user value is used as-is and not scaled. RAPL / hwmon — zmrig --report reads it when the kernel exposes it. That is package power; add 15–30 W for the rest, which is what the two settings are for. Guessing from TDP — 30–50 % error is normal. Some machines will simply need the meter. The pwsrc field in a code says where the number came from. If it says none, type one.

documents.t: One 2 vCPU machine, 814 H/s, 45 W package, PSU 87 %, 25 W overhead, electricity at $0.10/kWh: W wall = 45 / 0.87 + 25 = 76.7 W energy = 76.7 × 24 / 1000 = 1.84 kWh/day cost = 1.84 × 0.10 = $0.184/day revenue = 0.814 × 0.000096 × $300 = $0.0234/day profit = 0.0234 − 0.184 = −$0.16/day That is the honest answer for a rented VPS at European electricity prices: mining Monero on a general-purpose CPU loses money. A machine you already own, whose power is free or nearly free, is a different calculation — and that is the case this software is built for. What the calculator cannot know Network difficulty, coin price and share luck move constantly. Everything here is an estimate built on your miner's measurements; the only hard numbers are the hashrate and, when --power is used, the watts.

A report code is how a machine describes itself without a server: one line of text, printable on a console, pasteable into chat, readable in a browser. sudo ./oneclick.sh report --power 45 ZMRIG1.eyJ2IjoxLCJpZCI6InZwc… # while mining: keep the file fresh zmrig --report-file /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt --report-interval 60 sudo cat /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt

ZMRIG1. followed by base64url of a compact JSON object. Version 1 of the format: { "v": 1, "id": "vps-sg-02", "ver": "6.32.1", "cpu": "AMD EPYC 7B13 64-Core Processor", "arch": "x86_64", "cores": 32, "thr": 2, "algo": "rx/0", "mode": "fast", "hs": [1461.2, 1470.5, 1466.1, 1478.9], "hp": [1168, 1168], "shares": [806, 0, 0], "hash": 881234012, "up": 86400, "pw": 22, "pwsrc": "rapl", "hw": 66.8, "tmax": 72, "tc": 68.5, "at": 7, "health": "ok", "pool": "gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001", "ts": 1793412000 } Field Meaning hs hashrate over 10 s, 60 s, 15 min, session best (H/s) hp huge pages granted, needed shares accepted, rejected, failed hash total hashes computed up uptime in seconds pw, pwsrc watts, and the source: rapl, hwmon, user, none hw hashes per watt, when power is known, else null tmax the --max-temp target, or null when no thermal policy is armed tc the temperature the governor last acted on, or null at threads currently allowed to hash — below thr while it is throttling health the miner's view of its own income: ok, warming, degraded, stalled, rejected at below thr is the one field a fleet dashboard cannot derive from hashrate: a throttled rig and a healthy rig at half load look identical from the pool side, and only one of them has a bearing on its way out. Nothing else is in it. No wallet address, no pool password, no public IP, no hostname beyond the worker name you chose yourself.

cut -d. -f2 report.txt | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d | python3 -m json.tool Or in a browser console: JSON.parse(atob("eyJ2Ijox…".replace(/-/g, "+").replace(/_/g, "/"))) You should not have to trust a decoder on a website to read a number your own machine produced. The calculator on this site decodes locally and sends nothing, but the two lines above are the whole trick.

--report measures a 10 s warm-up plus a window of --report-time seconds (15 by default), then reports the stable hashrate rather than the average since startup: an average would include the dataset build and come out 20–25 % low. In the calculator you pick the window: Window Use it for 10 s the current state of the machine 60 s the default; smooths brief dips 15 min a thermal-throttled or shared host session best what the machine can do when nothing else is running Comparing machines on different windows is the fastest way to draw a wrong conclusion about a CPU.

Give each machine a distinct --report-id. Let the miner keep writing its report file. Collect the lines and paste them into the calculator one per line — or as raw JSON, if you keep your own inventory. Codes survive copy-paste: the alphabet is base64url, so no line breaks, spaces or shell quoting are needed.

The bot is the fast path. Sometimes a page is the right shape: a laptop on the sofa, a phone at work, somebody who is not in your chat. The same fleet, the same commands, rendered as HTML — and off until you ask for it. FLEET_WEB_PASSWORD='at-least-twelve-characters' That is the whole configuration. With it set, GET / is the overview. With it empty, no HTML exists at all: / stays the read-only status page and every dashboard path answers 404. One password, one operator. No accounts, no email, no invites, nothing to leak on somebody else's server.

path / fleet total: hashrate, rigs mining, offline count, hottest, and what needs attention /rigs one row per machine: state, hashrate, temperature, last seen /rig/<id> everything about one rig, plus its controls /enrol the three-step enrolment, with your URL already filled in /downloads the current ISO and its checksum, straight from the releases API /docs the commands the bot accepts, for reference A rig page carries what the chat carries: Start, Stop, Restart, Update, Fetch log, Reboot, a wallet-and-pool form, a coin / mode / heat-cap / threads / worker form, rename, and remove. Everything is queued — the rig applies it on its next check-in, 60 seconds by default, and reports the result back to the page and to the chat. Nothing is pushed down a live connection, so a click in a browser cannot wedge a miner mid-share. Two rules that surprise people: An empty wallet or pool field means leave it alone, never "clear it". Changing a wallet means typing a different one. A rig enrolled in the browser belongs to the primary chat admin, so /devices in Telegram lists it next to everything else.

On the machine: zmrig-os fleet --url https://your-fleet.onrender.com zmrig-os id device ZMR-1A2B-3C4D-5E6F enrol code ABCD-1234 Then /enrol, two fields, one optional name. The code is derived from the rig's own key and is verified server-side, so a stolen Device ID cannot be enrolled without somebody standing at the machine. zmrig-os sync --now makes it appear immediately instead of within a minute.

Pages are rendered by the server from the same store the bot writes to, then cached in memory until the fleet's revision counter moves. A refresh with no new check-ins does not touch the templating code. 5.3 KB of CSS, under 1 KB of JS, both immutable and cached for a year. No font, no framework, no third-party request of any kind. Brotli or gzip when the browser asks and the page is over 512 bytes, plus an ETag and 304 Not Modified — a phone on mobile data refreshes the fleet for a few hundred bytes. It is the same Node process as the bot. Nothing extra to host, nothing extra to pay for, and killing the dashboard does not stop the bot.

documents.t: the password is compared with timingSafeEqual against FLEET_WEB_PASSWORD; ten failed logins from one address in fifteen minutes ⇒ 429 for that address; every form carries a CSRF token bound to the session; a form without one is 403 and changes nothing; the session cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, seven days, and Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS; Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none' — no third-party script, font or image can load, so a compromised CDN cannot watch your fleet; the password lives in the environment, never in the repository, never in the state file, and it is not printed at startup. Serve it over HTTPS. On Render that is automatic; anywhere else, put it behind a reverse proxy, because a password typed into plain HTTP is a password on the wire.

scripts/latest-iso.sh asks the GitHub releases API and downloads the current image for your CPU: ./scripts/latest-iso.sh # newest stable, your CPU's variant ./scripts/latest-iso.sh --beta # newest beta ./scripts/latest-iso.sh --arch v3 # force x86-64-v3 ./scripts/latest-iso.sh --json # just the facts, for a script It prints the checksum and the size and leaves the comparison to sha256sum -c; it needs node (which the rig already has) and falls back to printing the releases page when it is missing. The same table is at /downloads on the dashboard. The full operator manual — every environment variable, the wire protocol, what each alert means — is doc/FLEET.md.

documents.t: This repository contains both sides: the miner (zmrig, xmrig) and a Monero pool written in Node.js with no dependencies, under pool/. Running your own pool means the pool fee stays with you instead of going to a stranger — and your miners point at it exactly as they would at any other pool.

Item Value Pool fee 1.0 % of each block, taken before splitting, rounded down Hidden fees none Miner developer fee 1 % of Monero mining time on the Zig engine (--donate-level=0 turns it off); the C++ engine takes nothing Payout threshold 0.01 XMR, plus the network fee The fee appears in the login reply the miner prints, in /api/config, and on the status page. Why 1 %: large Monero pools sit at 0.6–1 %, and this one does something most do not — it re-hashes every share with zmrig --verify-share before paying for it. That costs the operator real CPU, and it is the only thing that lets a miner know nobody is being paid for work they did not do.
documents.s: The 1 % fee, and what it buys

documents.t: # 1. a Monero node (testnet is fine while setting up) monerod --data-dir ~/.bitmonero --rpc-bind-ip 127.0.0.1 --confirm-external-bind # 2. the pool cd pool node src/index.js --check --config config.json # validate the config, then exit node src/index.js --config config.json # stratum + HTTP # 3. a miner, in another terminal zmrig -o 127.0.0.1:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4 http://127.0.0.1:8080/ is the status page; curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/stats returns the same numbers as JSON.

Node.js ≥ 18.17 — no npm install, no database. monerod with JSON-RPC reachable. zmrig in PATH so shares can be re-hashed. Without it the pool refuses shares rather than trusting them blindly: ./zmrig/build.sh --jobs 2 sudo install -m 0755 zmrig/out/zmrig /usr/local/bin/zmrig

A share is accepted only when the pool's own hash of the blob matches the hash the miner sent. A wrong hash is not merely rejected: the connection is closed. Share weight is difficulty × time, not share count — a slow machine is not punished and splitting one rig into three does not pay twice. Every block is written to audit.jsonl: reward, fee, each miner's payout, and the dust remainder listed on its own line instead of quietly folded into the fee. curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/audit?limit=5 | python3 -m json.tool curl -s 127.0.0.1:8080/api/worker/4YourMoneroAddress

Where How Notes Render render.yaml (Docker) single port, WebSocket only; a free instance sleeps after 15 minutes idle Fly.io fly.toml + a 1 GB volume real TCP on 3333; monerod does not fit in 256 MB Cloudflare Workers pool/worker/ WebSocket ⇄ TCP bridge, no Durable Object needed Vercel static page only a function cannot hold a stratum connection fly launch --no-deploy --copy-config --dockerfile deploy/Dockerfile fly volumes create pool_data --size 1 fly secrets set DAEMON=https://node.example:18081 fly deploy Point a miner at it over WebSocket (requires the zmrig engine), or over TCP when the host exposes port 3333: zmrig -o wss://pool.example.com/stratum -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4 zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress.rig1 -t 4

Keep state_file on a volume. Without it, a restart loses every miner's balance. /metrics exports Prometheus; /healthz returns 503 until a job template arrives from monerod. The audit log is append-only — rotate it with logrotate, never edit it. Change the fee wallet with OPERATOR_ADDRESS; the default lives in pool/src/operator.js. --check refuses configurations that cannot pay correctly: a fee outside 0–10 %, an unknown mode, a PPLNS window that is too short. Payouts via monero-wallet-rpc, the API and the security notes are in pool/README.md, and the deployment steps you must run yourself are in doc/SETUP.md.

Ten rigs in two buildings, one wallet, one connection to the pool. proxy/ does that: Node 18+, no dependencies, nothing to compile. sudo ./proxy/install.sh --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 Or without installing anything: node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 install.sh --dry-run prints the systemd unit before writing it, and the banner prints the exact line each rig has to run.

Three ways a farm loses money, all with the same root: Duplicated work. A Monero nonce is 32 bits. Two rigs searching the same range means a share only gets paid once. The proxy gives each rig its own top nonce byte and keeps the bottom 24 bits for the rig — the same scheme as xmrig-proxy. The trap: prefix 0 is not a prefix. A blob with nonce 0 is the miner's signal to turn extranonce mode off, so handing a rig 0 silently puts it back into the shared range and earns less. One difficulty for every rig. A 500 H/s machine and a 20 kH/s machine on the same target produce one share an hour and one a minute. The small rig starves while still using full power. The proxy assigns difficulty per rig, targeting about 15 seconds per share. A login storm. The pool sees one login per rig, and a pool behind Cloudflare — or any free-tier service — rate-limits logins and then bans the IP. One connection from the proxy covers the farm, while each rig still shows up as its own worker (--user=wallet.rig3). The proxy does not hash. It checks each share's target (a BigInt comparison, microseconds) and forwards it; the pool re-hashes. It cannot fake work, and this implementation does not try.

node proxy/src/main.js doctor --user=4YourMoneroAddress --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 ok pool gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 answered -- 168 ms ok job difficulty -- 60011.2 ok a 5 kH/s rig would find -- 0.30 shares/hour at this difficulty The last line is the calculation people skip: shares per hour is hashrate × 3600 / difficulty. 0.30 means one share every three hours — fine for a long-window PPLNS pool, fatal for one with a high payout threshold.

documents.t: Flag Transport Stable address Third party Verdict --tunnel=wireguard WireGuard over UDP, in the kernel 10.66.66.1 none use this --tunnel=tailscale WireGuard via a coordination server *.ts.net Tailscale good when nothing can be forwarded --tunnel=cf named Cloudflare tunnel, WebSocket your hostname Cloudflare works, one more edge hop --tunnel=cf-quick *.trycloudflare.com, WebSocket random, new every run Cloudflare demo only # once, on the machine that runs the proxy node proxy/src/main.js tunnel wireguard --rigs=10 --dir=wg sudo cp wg/ocean-proxy.conf /etc/wireguard/ocean-proxy.conf sudo systemctl enable --now wg-quick@ocean-proxy node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 --tunnel=wireguard That writes the server config plus one file per rig (wg/rig-1.conf …), each with its own key and an address from 10.66.66.2 upward, and an INSTALL.txt with the copy commands. One file per machine — sharing a file is the WireGuard version of the duplicate-nonce bug. Why this is the default recommendation: stable addresses (a changed ISP address requires no rig edits), UDP handled in the kernel so no added latency, no third party, and only one UDP port (51820) opened on the router — the stratum port stays on localhost.

node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 \ --tunnel=tailscale --tunnel-token=tskey-auth-… Three things to know before choosing it: Funnel only serves 443/8443/10000, TLS only, and its bandwidth is not enough to poll a dashboard every second (it is plenty for stratum, a few kB/s). The free Personal plan is non-commercial. If the rigs are in the same tailnet, skip Funnel entirely and point them at <host>.<tailnet>.ts.net:3333; nothing is exposed to the internet.

documents.t: A quick tunnel is not a production path. It is good for exactly one thing: proving in two minutes that the network works. Property Consequence for mining Random hostname every start every rig needs updating after every restart No uptime commitment a dropped tunnel stops every rig at once No access control anyone with the name can mine to your wallet One more hop added latency on every job notification A named tunnel with a token fixes the hostname and the access control, and it is the right choice when only 443 is allowed. Even then the proxy stays the only thing exposed, and the rigs never see the internet.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3334/status | python3 -m json.tool /status reports, per rig, the hashrate derived from accepted shares and the local difficulty it was given, plus XMR/day when the network difficulty is known: node proxy/src/main.js start --user=4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool=gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 \ --network-difficulty=350000000000 --block-reward=0.6 The figure is measured, not inferred from a CPU name, and it is null rather than a guess when the network difficulty is unknown.

A rig prints a Device ID and an enrolment code on its console. Type them into the bot once, and that machine is yours to configure from the chat: wallet, pool, coin, mining mode, heat cap, thread count, worker name. It reports back — hashrate, temperature, uptime, the log on request — and alerts you when it goes quiet. # on the rig, once zmrig-os fleet --url https://your-fleet.onrender.com zmrig-os id device ZMR-1A2B-3C4D-5E6F enrol code ABCD-1234 # in the chat /enroll ZMR-1A2B-3C4D-5E6F ABCD-1234 basement /wallet ZMR-1A2B-3C4D-5E6F 4YourMoneroAddress... That is the whole onboarding. The wallet is typed once, in the chat, for as many rigs as you own.

Command /enroll <id> <code> [name] link a rig to you /devices every rig: state, hashrate, temperature, last seen /status one screen: rigs, total hashrate, hottest, offline count /device <rig> one rig, with buttons /wallet <rig> 4… set the wallet, validated before it is queued /pool <rig> host:port set the pool /coin <rig> xmr|wow|arq|graft|sfx|yada|xla set the coin /mode <rig> max|balanced|eco|light|safe [C] aggression, and a heat cap /threads <rig> 8|auto pin the thread count /worker <rig> name the name the pool sees /update <rig> newest miner; the OS goes into the spare A/B slot /log <rig> [n] the rig's last lines, with the next check-in /reboot <rig> /rename /remove the rest <rig> is the full ID, a unique part of it (3C4D), or the name you gave it. Changes are queued, not pushed: a rig that is offline right now receives them when it comes back, and every result — applied or refused — is reported in the chat. zmrig-os validates everything again on the machine, so a hand-built request to the control plane cannot talk a rig into a wallet it would reject.

a rig that has not checked in for five minutes; a rig that came back; temperature at or above 85 °C; the miner stopping when it was mining; hashrate below half of the previous check-in; hashrate below half of the rate the rig measured on itself, which catches the machine that has been sliding for a week rather than the one that fell over just now; every command result, including refusals. Each kind has a cooldown per rig, so a hot machine does not shout every minute. The second hashrate rule is the slow one, and it says what it compared: 🐌 rig-2 is at 640.0 H/s, 45% of the 1.4 kH/s it measured itself

One Node process, no dependencies, one JSON file of state. cd fleet cp config.example.env .env # TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, FLEET_ADMIN_IDS set -a; . ./.env; set +a npm run check # prints the config, opens no socket npm start fleet/render.yaml is a Render blueprint. On the free plan the instance sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, so point a free uptime monitor at /healthz every 5 minutes — a sleeping bot answers nothing, though the rigs keep mining and catch up when it wakes. The token lives in an environment variable, never in a file in the repository. Your own id is the only one the bot answers until you add more to FLEET_ADMIN_IDS.

ZMR-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX sha256(key)[0..6), upper case enrol code XXXX-XXXX sha256("enroll:" + key)[0..4), upper case The 32-byte key is generated on the rig and never leaves it. The server recomputes both strings from the key presented on every check-in, so an ID cannot be claimed by a machine that does not hold its key, and the code proves the machine is in front of you. Nothing connects to a rig: it calls out, once a minute, and everything else waits for that call. On a live stick the key lives in RAM — install to disk, or give the stick a ZMRIGDATA partition with zmrig-os persist, or the rig reports a new ID after a reboot.

Leave FLEET_URL empty and nothing changes: the rig never contacts anything, and zmrig-os setup remains the way to configure it. The control plane is an addition, not a dependency. Operator-level detail — every environment variable, the wire format, the failure modes — is in doc/FLEET.md.

You choose The installer receives Coin --algo rx/wow — Monero adds nothing, because a switching pool may move the rig Wallet --wallet <address> Rig name --rig-id <name> Pool --pool <host:port> or --pool tls://<host:port> Backup pools --failover <host:port>,<host:port> Fixed engine --engine zmrig or --engine xmrig (absent = automatic) Fixed profile --profile free or --profile watt (absent = automatic) 443-only network --cloudflare --ws-path <path> Proxy --proxy <url> Pool name filtered here --connect-to <host:port> Host refuses MSR writes --no-msr Rented hash --nicehash Do not tune the host --no-tune No thread search --no-autotune Keep the config (no --force) Two rules are worth knowing because they change the command rather than just adding a flag: Asking for WebSocket or a proxy forces --engine zmrig. The C++ engine has no WebSocket client and no proxy support, so the alternative would be a config nothing can run. A TLS pool becomes part of the --pool value (tls://host:port), because that is the form oneclick.sh parses. The address you type is validated before the copy button unlocks: for Monero, 95 characters, 106 for an integrated address, base58 alphabet only. For the other six coins the check is the alphabet and a plausible length, plus a warning when the prefix is not the one this site knows — it does not pretend to verify a checksum it never computes. A pool host is validated as host:port, and a full stratum+tcp://… URL pasted from a provider page is accepted. The coin decides two things. It pins the algorithm (--algo rx/wow and so on) — except for Monero, where adding the flag would stop a switching pool from moving the rig to whichever RandomX coin pays best. And it decides whether a pool preset is offered: the seven presets are Monero pools, so every other coin asks you for its endpoint instead of inventing one. Other coins has the details and the commands. The proxy field wants the whole URL — socks5://host:port or http://user:pass@host:port — because that is what the miner parses. The dial address is host:port only; it replaces the resolved IP but keeps the pool's hostname in SNI and the Host header, which is the point: a name blocked by a local resolver still works if you know where it lives.

The preview button copies the same command with plan in place of install. plan resolves the pool, the engine, the profile, the huge-page strategy and the autotune plan, prints them, and stops. It writes nothing. Neither command contains your wallet's private anything: a public address is the only credential involved, and it is visible to the pool by design.

Both engines compile to the same hash loop: zmrig/capi binds the C++ RandomX implementation into the Zig binary, so the numbers are the same within noise. The difference is everything around the loop. xmrig (C++) zmrig (Zig) Algorithms all of them (34+) the RandomX family: rx/0, rx/wow, rx/arq, rx/graft, rx/sfx, rx/yada, panthera (rx/2 parses but no coin uses it and it is not tested) Transports TCP, TLS TCP, TLS, ws, wss Proxy partial SOCKS5 HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS5, with auth and remote DNS Monitoring API yes, complete yes, read-only, XMRig-compatible shape Report code for the calculator no yes (--report) Health watchdog no yes, restarts when earnings stop Measured rx/0 832 H/s 800–841 H/s, same host, same config Both are measured on the same 2 vCPU machine, --bench, 2 MiB pages; the spread is the host, not the engine. Benchmarks has the method. Every algorithm above has a reference vector in zmrig --self-test, so the Zig engine's coverage is checked rather than claimed.

RandomX on a normal VPS: either. zmrig is smaller, has the transport options and prints a report code, so it is what the installer picks. A switching pool (MoneroOcean and clones): zmrig still works — it advertises the whole RandomX family and the pool moves the rig between coins. It cannot mine the non-RandomX algorithms those pools also pay for, so a pool that values breadth more than depth is better served by xmrig. The installer's auto setting chooses xmrig for a switching pool for this reason; zmrig stays the default either way (1 % of Monero time, switchable off). Any other algorithm (cn/heavy, ghostrider, KawPow): xmrig. zmrig refuses at argument-parse time rather than starting and failing to connect. A network that only allows 443, or a proxy: zmrig. See Networks that only allow 443.

The engine is recorded in /etc/zmrig/engine, so later subcommands (status, logs, bench, …) use the same binary without repeating --engine. sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --engine zmrig --force sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --engine xmrig --force Both binaries can stay installed side by side; the service runs whichever the marker names.
oneclick.sh [subcommand] [options] The default subcommand is install when a wallet is given and status when it is not.

Subcommand What it does install dependencies, build, tune, config, service, self-check (default) build compile only; keeps the previous binary until the new one links tune huge pages, THP, governor, MSR — root only config (re)generate /etc/zmrig/config.json without touching the service start, stop, restart, status, logs service control bench reproducible RandomX measurement (--bench=20000) report measure and print a ZMRIG1. code for the calculator verify self-test, then audit the developer fee (rate, address, off switch) plan print every automatic decision and change nothing update fetch the configured branch, rebuild, restart uninstall stop, remove service and binaries, keep the config purge remove everything the tool ever created

Flag Meaning --force overwrite an existing config --yes never prompt (unattended installs) --no-service install and configure, do not create a unit --all-backends also build OpenCL/CUDA support --build-dir DIR where to compile (default /usr/local/src/zmrig-build)

Path What /usr/local/bin/zmrig the Zig miner /usr/local/bin/xmrig the C++ miner, when that engine is selected /usr/local/bin/zmrig-tune host tuning (--status, --hugepages 1G, --algo panthera sizes the reservation for that coin, …) /usr/local/bin/zmrig-bench reproducible hashrate measurement /usr/local/bin/zmrig-verify the developer-fee audit /etc/zmrig/config.json configuration, mode 600 /var/lib/zmrig/ state and the report file zmrig.service the miner: Restart=always, RestartSec=5, Nice=-10, LimitMEMLOCK=infinity, PrivateTmp=true zmrig-tune.service oneshot tuner, runs before the miner at boot http://127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary read-only monitoring API

Up to installer 1.2 the tool installed itself as xmrig-ocean. A new install does not silently leave the old one behind: /etc/xmrig-ocean/config.json is copied to /etc/zmrig/config.json (mode 600) if the new path does not exist yet. /var/lib/xmrig-ocean is moved to /var/lib/zmrig. The old unit is stopped, disabled and removed, so the machine does not end up running two miners after a reboot. purge removes both name sets, so an upgrade does not leave orphan files.

ALPHA ──► BETA ──► master newest default upstream history Every command in these pages uses BETA. To try ALPHA once: MINER_BRANCH=ALPHA sudo -E ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress sudo ./oneclick.sh update # back to the default branch update fetches the configured branch before checking it out, and stops with the branch name if it does not exist. That used to fail quietly.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MoLik-Labs/ZMRIG/BETA/oneclick.sh \ | sudo bash -s -- --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress If the repository is already cloned: sudo ./oneclick.sh --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress That is the whole install. It installs the build dependencies, compiles the hash engine and the miner, measures the machine to pick a thread count, tunes the host, writes /etc/zmrig/config.json, creates zmrig.service, runs a self-check, and prints the hashrate it measured. Re-running is safe: no duplicate services, no overwritten config without --force, no rebuild when the binary is newer than the sources.

Decision How the installer chooses Engine zmrig (1 % of Monero time, --donate-level=0 to remove it). It advertises the whole RandomX family, so a switching pool can still move the rig to whichever coin pays best. --algo outside RandomX, or --engine=xmrig, selects the C++ engine, which takes nothing. Profile free (maximum hashrate) everywhere, except a laptop on battery → watt (maximum hashes per watt). Threads Measured after the build: each candidate runs 8 s on the real dataset, the winner is written to the config. Huge pages Sized from the dataset. If the kernel grants fewer, it falls back to transparent huge pages and says so. Governor performance for free, the existing powersave governor for watt. See the same list without touching the machine: ./oneclick.sh plan ==> plan engine zmrig (RandomX family, 1% dev fee) pool gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 algo auto (RandomX family: rx/0, rx/wow, rx/arq, …) profile free (auto: no battery, electricity is treated as free) mode auto (fast when RAM allows) huge pages none yet, the installer reserves what the dataset needs autotune 8 s per candidate, winner written to config.json service zmrig.service (systemd)

sudo ./oneclick.sh status # service, hashrate 10s/60s/15m, shares, huge pages sudo ./oneclick.sh verify # self-test + developer-fee audit sudo ./oneclick.sh logs 50 # last 50 log lines ==> verifying zmrig OK PASS rx/0 reference vector OK PASS pipelined hashing OK PASS full-memory dataset matches the cache OK fee audit: one wallet, Monero only, switchable off OK verified status only reports measured numbers: a miner that started a moment ago says warming up instead of quoting the previous run, because the dataset takes 15–25 seconds to build.

# free electricity: café, school, an office machine — maximum hashrate sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --profile free # every watt costs money: laptop, metered VPS — maximum hashes per watt sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --profile watt free uses every logical CPU, --mode fast, huge pages and --priority 5. watt drops to one thread per physical core (SMT adds 5–15 % hashrate for 30–40 % more power), does not pin the CPU to its highest clock, and stops by itself when a laptop switches to battery.

sudo ./oneclick.sh update # git pull, rebuild, restart sudo ./oneclick.sh uninstall # stop, remove service and binary, keep the config sudo ./oneclick.sh purge --dry-run sudo ./oneclick.sh purge # remove everything the tool created purge prints every path it created with its size, requires the word purge to confirm, resets vm.nr_hugepages to 0, and never touches a file it did not make. --dry-run lists without deleting.

No huge pages. In a container or an OpenVZ VPS the kernel may refuse; the miner logs the shortfall and continues at roughly 78 % hashrate. Nothing to fix — ask the host for 2 MiB pages. Service restarts in a loop. Almost always a config the miner rejects. Run sudo journalctl -u zmrig -n 60 and look for the first line after the binary starts; the installer validates the config before writing it, so this usually means someone edited it. the miner rejected the generated config. The wallet contains a character that is not valid base58. Re-run with a clean address. The rest of the failure modes are in Troubleshooting.

ZMRIG is a complete Monero mining setup, not a collection of scripts: Part What it is What it costs Miner XMRig 6.26.0 with every line of donation code removed, plus a complete Zig miner on the same RandomX engine 1 % of Monero time on the Zig engine, printed and switchable off; the C++ engine has no fee code Installer oneclick.sh: one flag, host tuning, systemd unit, self-check, purge free Proxy one pool connection for a farm: extranonce per rig, per-rig difficulty, tunnels free Pool self-hosted Monero pool: stratum over TCP and WebSocket, PPLNS, every share verified 1 % of each block, nothing else The miner works with any pool. The 1 % on the pool in this repository is what keeps the project running; the miner itself takes nothing either way, and there is no account, token or telemetry anywhere in it.

The fee is provable, so it is checked. sudo ./oneclick.sh verify greps the binary for the upstream donation endpoints and known wallets, then runs hash self-tests so that "it found nothing" cannot mean "it looked at the wrong file". See the fee page for the rate, the log lines and how to turn it off. There are no flags to start. --wallet is the only required input. The installer reads the CPU, the RAM, the hypervisor and the battery, then picks the engine, the thread count, the huge-page strategy and the governor, and prints the reason for each choice before it acts. ./oneclick.sh plan shows every decision and changes nothing. A miner that is not earning should say so. A rig whose pool rejects every share looks perfectly healthy from outside. zmrig judges its own numbers once a second and exits so the supervisor restarts it — twenty seconds of lost hashrate instead of a night of zero.

documents.t: Linux x86-64 (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Fedora, Arch; the script detects the distro). macOS and Windows can build the C++ engine, but the installer targets Linux. 2 GB of free RAM for fast mode, or --mode light with about 300 MB. systemd if you want it as a service. root, for huge pages, MSR and the service. A network connection for the first build. Everything is compiled on the machine; no binary is downloaded from anywhere.
