Install in one command — the five minutes most people need. Choosing an engine — zmrig or xmrig. Pools and money — fees, minimums, and how not to get an IP banned. Profitability calculator — paste the codes your machines print.

Two ways to get numbers out of the miner: HTTP API Report code Use when the machine is on your network or VPN, or a script needs it the machine is behind NAT, or you want a number in a spreadsheet Security binds 127.0.0.1, optional Bearer token opens no port; you copy the code yourself Data everything, updated every second a snapshot at the moment it was written Many machines one endpoint each paste several codes at once

Enabled by --http-port; the installer turns it on at 18080. curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary curl -s 127.0.0.1:18080/2/summary | python3 -m json.tool Path Content /1/summary, /summary compact single-line JSON, XMRig shape /1/status connection state /2/summary, /2/status same data, pretty-printed /json_rpc same as /1/summary, for older clients zmrig ... --http-port 18080 --http-access-token "$TOKEN" curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 127.0.0.1:18080/1/summary A missing token returns 401 with JSON, an unknown path 404 with JSON, HEAD works for health checks, and every response carries Cache-Control: no-store. {"id":"zmrig","worker_id":"vps-sg-02","uptime":3600,"version":"6.32.1", "kind":"miner","ua":"zmrig/6.32.1","algo":"rx/0","paused":false, "donate_level":0, "connection":{"pool":"wss://relay.example.com:443","uptime":3600,"failures":0,"tls":true}, "hashrate":{"total":[814.2,810.5,805.1],"highest":902.7}, "hugepages":[1168,1168],"cpu":{"threads":2}, "results":{"shares_good":42,"shares_total":42,"hashes_total":2931842,"error_log":[]}} The API is read-only: there is no endpoint that changes a wallet or restarts anything. Even so, do not bind it to 0.0.0.0 without a token and a firewall — it reveals the worker name, the pool and your address.

That is a different question from "is the service active", and it is where money disappears quietly: a pool that rejects every share leaves a miner that is running, connected, printing hashrate, and earning nothing. The miner judges itself once a second and reports one of five states: State Meaning What happens warming building the dataset, or paused nothing (pausing is a feature) ok hashrate near this session's best, shares accepted nothing degraded below 80 % of the 10-minute peak (heat, a noisy neighbour) warning stalled the process is alive but not hashing error rejected shares were sent and none were accepted error sudo ./oneclick.sh status # hashrate: 1042.6 H/s (10s/60s/15m) # shares: 184/0/0 accepted # health: ok stalled or rejected for 15 minutes makes the process exit with code 3, and Restart=always turns that into a clean start. The trade is explicit: 16–30 seconds of lost hashrate instead of hours of earning zero. zmrig ... --no-health-restart # never exit on its own zmrig ... --health-restart=1800 # wait longer before giving up (seconds) zmrig ... --health-warmup=300 # ignore the first 5 minutes The state is also in the health field of a report code, so a fleet table can show the machines that are running and earning nothing.
documents.s: Health: still running, or still earning?

documents.t: One measurement, one line: $ sudo ./oneclick.sh report --power 45 ZMRIG1.eyJ2IjoxLCJpZCI6InZwc… # about 380–520 characters It takes 25–30 seconds: 15–20 s to build the dataset, 10 s of warm-up, 15 s of measurement, then a power sample. oneclick.sh report stops the service first — the running miner holds the huge pages, and a second dataset does not fit. Field Meaning id, cpu, cores, thr machine name, CPU model, physical cores, mining threads algo, mode algorithm, auto/fast/light hs[0..3] hashrate over 10 s, 60 s, 15 min, session best hp huge pages granted / needed shares, hash, up accepted, rejected, failed; total hashes; uptime in seconds pw, pwsrc watts and where they came from: rapl/hwmon (CPU package), user (wall meter), none pool, ts, ver pool, timestamp, miner version A code contains no wallet address, no pool token, no public IP. It is base64url-encoded JSON and you can read it yourself: cut -d. -f2 report.txt | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d | python3 -m json.tool While mining, let the miner keep the file fresh: --report-file /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt --report-interval 60 The installer enables that for the zmrig engine, so a later sudo cat /var/lib/zmrig/report.txt is enough.

Give each machine its own --report-id (or --rig-id). Let the miner write its report file. Paste the codes into the profitability calculator, one per line. The calculator totals hashrate, watts, kWh, power cost, revenue and profit, and exports JSON. There is no intermediate server. For 24/7 monitoring, scrape the API into Prometheus or Netdata over your own VPN; do not expose it to the internet.
documents.s: From one code to a fleet

documents.t: A "picky" VPS usually lands in one of four situations: Only outbound 443/tcp; 3333, 10001, 5555 are blocked. TLS required, plaintext stratum dropped, or DPI cutting unfamiliar packets. Everything must go through the organisation's proxy. Only certain address ranges are reachable (a CDN's anycast, an internal relay). The Zig engine handles all four. The C++ engine has no WebSocket client, so it cannot handle (1) and most of (2) — the installer switches engines rather than writing a config that cannot connect.

sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool my-relay.example.com \ --cloudflare=my-relay.example.com --ws-path /pool --cloudflare means: wss://<host>:443<path>, TLS on, engine zmrig. Forcing --engine xmrig alongside it is refused, not silently ignored. The same thing by hand: zmrig -o wss://my-relay.example.com:443/pool -u 4YourMoneroAddress -p x
documents.s: One flag for the common case

documents.t: If the pool publishes a WebSocket endpoint on 443, no. If it does not, something has to bridge WebSocket to raw stratum. Two options that work: Relay When it fits Cost pool/worker/ in this repository the pool speaks plain TCP and you want a wss:// endpoint free Workers plan is enough for a farm Your own Worker you want to read every line of it free Workers plan The Worker in pool/worker/ is a byte pipe: it opens a TCP socket to the pool and pipes frames both ways. It does not see your wallet, and the pool sees the Worker's address, not your VPS. It does see the stratum traffic, which is why self-hosting matters if that concerns you. # 1. cd pool/worker && edit wrangler.toml, then: npx wrangler deploy # 2. point the miner at it sudo ./oneclick.sh install --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress \ --pool your-worker.workers.dev --cloudflare \ --ws-path /relay/YOUR_TOKEN --yes

# SOCKS5, no auth zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress --proxy socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 # HTTP CONNECT with credentials zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --proxy http://user:pass@proxy.corp.example:3128 The Zig engine resolves the pool name through the proxy (remote DNS), so a poisoned local resolver does not matter.

Quad9 returns NXDOMAIN for gulf.moneroocean.stream; Cloudflare's malware resolver does the same for pool.supportxmr.com. A blocked name looks identical to a blocked port in a miner log. # keep the hostname for SNI and Host, dial a known-good address zmrig -o pool.example.com:3333 -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --connect-to 203.0.113.10:3333 # or pin the CA of your own relay zmrig -o wss://relay.example.com/pool -u 4YourMoneroAddress \ --tls-ca /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem The installer copies a CA you supply to /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem: the unit runs with PrivateTmp=true, so a file in /tmp can disappear on restart.
documents.s: When DNS is the problem, not the firewall

documents.t: Retry a wrong wallet every five seconds. A rejected wallet is identified, that pool is left alone for 30 minutes, and the log says what to fix. Reconnect immediately after your IP is banned. Fifteen minutes per pool (--ban-cooldown), then the next pool in the failover list. Keep submitting after three shares were called invalid — a ten-minute pause instead of the hour-long ban xmrpool.eu hands out. Let twenty rebooting rigs reconnect in the same millisecond. Every retry is jittered ±20 %. These are the behaviours that separate one bad evening from a permanent block. More on pool choice in Pools.
documents.s: What the miner will not do

documents.t: RandomX is a memory-bound proof of work: the hash loop reads a dataset in a random order. Almost everything that matters follows from that one sentence.

Huge pages. The largest and most obvious gain. A 4 KiB page size makes the dataset walk a TLB miss every few accesses. There are two ways to get 2 MiB pages and the miner reports which one it got: huge pages … MB (explicit) means the reserved pool, and huge pages: … MB via THP (…, measured by the kernel) means transparent huge pages collapsed the mapping — read from /proc/self/smaps_rollup, not assumed. The second is what an unprivileged user gets on a stock Ubuntu kernel, and it is worth most of the gain: 786 H/s against 615 H/s for 4 KiB pages on the test host, where the reserved pool gives 800–841. echo 1168 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages # ~2.3 GiB of 2 MiB pages, for Monero grep HugePages_ /proc/meminfo The installer does this and sets LimitMEMLOCK=infinity in the unit. The number is not a constant: it is the cache plus the dataset of the coin being mined — 1168 pages for Monero, 96 for Panthera/Scala (see the table below). zmrig sizes its own reservation per algorithm and zmrig-tune --algo= writes the same number, so sudo zmrig-tune --algo panthera reserves 192 MB and not 2.3 GB. To check the miner got them: the startup log prints how many bytes really came from explicit huge pages (huge pages 2336 MB (explicit)), and the API reports "hugepages": [granted, needed] — [1168, 1168] for rx/0, [96, 96] for panthera. Measuring without huge pages Once 1234 pages are reserved, only about 1.2 GB of ordinary RAM is left. Running --no-huge-pages then gets the process OOM-killed (exit 137), because a second 2 GiB dataset does not fit. Set nr_hugepages to 0 before measuring that case, and remember to put it back. Fast or light mode. fast builds one dataset shared by every thread. light keeps the cache and rebuilds every dataset line per hash: 82 H/s against 849 H/s on the same machine, same minute, rx/0 — a factor of ten, not a power-saving option. A rig that falls back to light mode is not mining, it is idling at 10 %. The startup log says which one it chose and why, and --check prints the decision before you start. Which one you get in --mode=auto depends on the coin, because the coins are not the same size. This is measured, not estimated from a constant: Algorithm Coin Cache Dataset Total Fits in 1 GiB VPS? rx/0 Monero 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only rx/wow Wownero 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only rx/arq ArQmA 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only rx/graft Graft 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only rx/sfx Safex Cash 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only rx/yada YadaCoin 256 MB 2080 MB 2336 MB light only panthera Scala (XLA) 128 MB 64 MB 192 MB yes The dataset size is the same for the six RandomX forks because they only change the program configuration, the argon salt and the iteration count; Panthera is a different configuration (ArgonMemory 128 MB, DatasetBaseSize 32 MB). zmrig --check prints the number for the algorithm you asked about, and the datasets are sized from the compiled configuration rather than from RANDOMX_DATASET_MAX_SIZE — that constant is 2 GiB and using it for a 64 MB dataset is how a 512 MB VPS ends up refusing to start on a coin it can mine. Threads. One per physical core, two per core only when SMT helps: on the test host, two threads on two vCPUs gave 808–817 H/s, one thread 408 H/s, and four threads on two cores 798–801 H/s — oversubscribing buys nothing. SMT usually adds 5–15 % hashrate for 30–40 % more power, which is why the watt profile drops it.

Scratchpad prefetch mode (0/1/2/3): 823, 814, 823, 814 H/s — inside noise. The default (1) stays. Affinity on a 2 vCPU machine: identical. It matters on a many-core box with an uneven L3, which is a different measurement. Anything advertised as a large speed-up that is not huge pages, dataset mode or thread count should be measured before it is believed.

2 vCPU Xeon at 2.60 GHz, 3.9 GiB RAM, 1234 × 2 MiB huge pages, algorithm rx/0, one run per configuration. Configuration Hashrate Ratio default: 2 threads, 1168 pages reserved, prefetch 1 800–841 H/s 100 % same, no pages reserved (THP backs the mapping) 786 H/s 95 % same, no pages reserved and THP off (4 KiB) 615–626 H/s 76 % --mode light 82 H/s 10 % -t 1 408 H/s 50 % -t 4 on two cores 798–801 H/s 98 % (noise) --scratchpad-prefetch=0/2/3 1208–1302 kH/s on panthera noise --no-affinity 814 H/s 100 % (noise) Re-checked for 6.33.0 on 2026-11-01 (three --bench=3000 runs, THP, two threads): 889 / 956 / 886 H/s — the same configuration as the 786 H/s row, different day. Treat the ratios, not the absolute numbers. The same binary on the same host in a quieter session measured 1008–1103 H/s. That 20–25 % spread is why absolute numbers in documentation are close to useless, and why the ratios above are the useful part. C++ engine on the same host, for reference: 1075.7 H/s. The gap to the Zig engine is smaller than the gap between two runs.

zmrig --bench=20000 # fixed seed, fixed blob, dataset build excluded zmrig --report --power 45 # 10 s warm-up + 15 s window, prints a code sudo ./oneclick.sh bench # stops the service first, then measures Rules that make a measurement mean something: Stop the miner first. A running miner holds the huge pages; the benchmark then allocates in ordinary memory and reports about 20 % low. Measure the machine you care about. Absolute hashrate is a property of the host, not of the binary. Run each configuration twice. Under 2 % is noise. The full table, with the dates and the caveats, is in Benchmarks.

Symptom Usual cause What to do dataset ready takes 20–30 s normal: building 2 GiB not a fault; --mode light takes 0.6 s but keeps 9 % of the hashrate. panthera builds 64 MB and is ready in about 0.4 s 20–30 % below expected hashrate the mapping is on 4 KiB pages zmrig --check prints the thp policy; the log must show 2 MiB pages, either huge pages … (explicit) or huge pages: … MB via THP (…, measured by the kernel) the process is killed, exit 137 out of RAM while building the dataset (huge pages already hold the rest) fix the huge-page reservation, or use --mode light cannot read …: check the path or run as root the config is root-only run with sudo config ok but nothing mines no -c, or no pool given --check only inspects the file it was given login failed: … repeats wrong wallet or pool, banned IP, wrong TLS mode read the line after it; try --transport tcp to rule TLS out connection lost repeatedly a CDN or NAT dropping a silent socket --keepalive-interval 60, --idle-timeout 120 share rejected: … stale job or difficulty, or the machine clock drifting check timedatectl; read the pool's own message API returns 401 an access token is configured send Authorization: Bearer TOKEN API unreachable from another machine it binds 127.0.0.1 by design do not expose it; use an SSH tunnel --tls-ca has no effect the file is in /tmp and the unit uses PrivateTmp put it at /etc/zmrig/tls-ca.pem

Light mode crashed on Panthera/Scala. The JIT snippet that reads the dataset masked the block number with Monero's 2 GiB mask, so a coin with a 32 MB dataset addressed memory it did not own, up to 2 GiB past the end of its 128 MB cache: SIGSEGV a fraction of a second after --check said the config was fine. The snippet is now patched with the mask of the algorithm at hand, the way the dataset-read path already was. Every algorithm has a reference vector in --self-test now, so this cannot come back quietly. Every algorithm was sized as Monero. The miner reserved 2416 MB of huge pages and refused to start without them, whatever the coin. Panthera needs 192 MB; a 512 MB VPS can mine it in fast mode. The reservation, the --mode=auto decision, the memory gate in front of --bench and zmrig-tune --algo all read the compiled configuration of the algorithm now. A bigger dataset was refused on a machine that had the memory. The pre-flight in front of --bench and --report compared the requirement against the huge-page pool and against MemAvailable separately, so a host that had followed the miner's own advice (echo 1168 > nr_hugepages) had 2336 MB in the pool and 1.2 GB of RAM, and the 2404 MB requirement matched neither number. The two are added now — the allocator falls back per mapping, so both are usable — and the message says which two figures it summed. Switching algorithm leaked 2.3 GiB. The cache was allocated with posix_memalign and freed with munmap, so the pages stayed mapped. A pool that rotates coins (MoneroOcean does) would run the machine out of memory after a handful of switches. Allocation and release now use the same path — mmap, so the memory is also never written twice before the dataset initialiser fills it. --background was ignored and the miner stayed in the foreground. It now forks, calls setsid and closes stdio. Reconnects were slow and then a storm. It waited the full --retry-pause after every drop and reset its counter on pool rotation, so a dead pool was hammered. Now: reconnect immediately after a session that had logged in, then 200 ms → 500 ms → 1 s → --retry-pause, with a counter that does not reset. Log files contained ANSI colour escapes. Files are plain text; stdout keeps colour. Command-line flags used to overwrite config values with defaults. zmrig -c config.json --verbose reset mode, huge-pages, retries. Only flags you actually type override now. report.enabled in the config started --report (measure, print, exit) instead of only writing the report file. The two are separate now. --tls used to imply "do not verify the certificate". It only selects the transport; verification stays on. One very long line from a pool killed the session. The line is dropped and warned about once when the session ends. --http-port never reached the config. Fixed; the installer writes the enabled boolean correctly. Ctrl-C hung while waiting for a login. The monitor closes the socket so the main thread can exit. A client that opened the API socket and went silent blocked the API thread. Every connection now has a 5-second timeout.
documents.s: Bugs that were fixed, so you do not have to meet them

documents.t: Is --mode light usable on a 1 GB VPS? It runs, at about 9 % of the hashrate (76 H/s against 814 H/s). Fine for keeping a connection or testing a config; for real mining, pick a VPS with at least 2.5 GB. How many threads? L3 cache / 2 MiB is right most of the time. If the VPS is throttled, drop one thread and measure again. Should a local pool use TLS? On the same machine or a private network, TLS costs CPU and adds no real security. Use it over the internet or through a CDN. Can it mine to several pools at once? Yes: several -o flags, or several entries in pools[]. It tries them in order and fails over after --retries failures. Does the API slow the miner down? No. It reads atomics that are updated once a second and never locks a worker. How long until the first share? Depends on pool difficulty: seconds on a test pool, minutes to hours on a real one with a small machine. A slow share is not a fault — check the hashrate and look for pool has been silent. How do I know the miner is mining to the right wallet? zmrig --check prints user=…, the API returns connection.pool, and the startup log prints wallet: …. Compare with the dashboard of the pool.

zmrig --version sudo ./oneclick.sh status sudo ./oneclick.sh logs 80 sed 's/"user": *"[^"]*"/"user": "REDACTED"/' /etc/zmrig/config.json Redact the wallet and any token before pasting. The log alone usually shows whether the failure is transport, TLS or the pool itself.

Two costs never show up on a hashrate chart: a pool paying less than it advertises, and an IP that can no longer connect. The first is a few percent; the second is 100 % of the income. Pool Fee Minimum payout Endpoint TLS on 443 Why MoneroOceanswitching 0 % 0.003 XMR gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 gulf.moneroocean.stream:443 Pays the most per hash: the pool moves the rig to whichever RandomX coin is paying best and settles in XMR. Needs --algo=auto, which is the default. SupportXMR 0.6 % 0.1 XMR pool.supportxmr.com:3333 pool.supportxmr.com:443 The largest pool, so blocks are found often and the daily number moves less. Pick it when you want a steady figure rather than the maximum. C3Pool 0 % 0.003 XMR c3pool.com:3333 no Zero fee and a low minimum like MoneroOcean, without algorithm switching. The best failover pool because the infrastructure is completely different. HeroMiners 0.9 % 0.01 XMR monero.herominers.com:10191 no The lowest minimum (0.01 XMR) among the fee-charging pools. Fine for a small rig, but 0.9 % comes out of the payout. xmrpool.eu 0.9 % 0.07 XMR xmrpool.eu:3333 xmrpool.eu:443 Has its own TLS port on 443 for filtered networks, but the strictest ban policy of the group: three bad shares means ten minutes, then an hour. zmrig stops before that line. P2Pool mini 0 % 0.0004 XMR pool.xmr.pub:3333 no No pool owner and no fee; pays out with every block found. The most frequent payouts and the most variance. P2Pool nano 0 % 0.0004 XMR pool.xmr.pub:3334 no The even lighter P2Pool sidechain: fits a 1 vCPU VPS, but fewer shares mean smaller, scarcer payouts. Fees and minimums checked October 2026. Short names work directly with the installer: --pool=moneroocean, supportxmr, c3pool, herominers, xmrpool, p2pool, p2pool-nano. To see exactly what the repository would use, without installing: ./oneclick.sh plan --pool=supportxmr --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress Other coins — Wownero, ArQmA, Graft, Safex Cash, YadaCoin, Scala — are covered in Other coins, including the ranking that says which one pays best for your hashrate.

MoneroOcean pays the most per hash on a CPU, because it moves the rig to whichever RandomX coin is paying best and settles in XMR. Independent measurements put the gap at 10-30 % against a single-algorithm pool, which is larger than every fee difference in the table. It needs --algo=auto, which is the default here. SupportXMR is the low-variance choice. The largest pool finds blocks often, so the daily number moves less. Pick it when a steady figure matters more than the maximum, or as the backup behind MoneroOcean. C3Pool is 0 % with a 0.003 XMR minimum — the same shape as MoneroOcean without algorithm switching, on completely different infrastructure. The best second backup. Fees and minimums were read from the pools' own pages in October 2026. Fees change; ports and ban policies change less.

A pool bans an IP for three reasons, and all three used to be invisible: Cause A naive miner This one Wrong wallet, wrong port, TLS in the wrong place retries every 5 s, forever, from the same IP identifies the refusal, skips that pool for 30 minutes, prints the fix your IP is banned reconnects at once and extends the ban 15 minutes per pool, then the next one An overclocked rig producing bad shares keeps submitting, earns a 10-minute ban, then an hour after three invalid shares, stops for 10 minutes and says why Twenty rigs rebooting at once identical timestamps, login flood every retry jittered ±20 % Cooldowns are per pool: a pool that refused your wallet does not block the backup. --ban-cooldown=<seconds> changes the default of 900; the wrong-wallet case is floored at 30 minutes, because waiting five seconds does not fix a typo.

Rigs lose their connection to DNS filtering more often than to a ban. Documented cases: Quad9 returns NXDOMAIN for gulf.moneroocean.stream, Cloudflare's malware resolver does the same for pool.supportxmr.com, some ISPs block mining domains wholesale, and many VPS or corporate networks allow only 80 and 443. Four ways through, in the order worth trying: A backup pool on another domain. --failover=moneroocean,c3pool writes the extra pools into config.json; they are used only when the first cannot be reached or refuses this IP. A regional hostname — the same pool, a different DNS name. That only helps when the default alias is the filtered one. Port 443 with TLS, which looks like ordinary HTTPS: MoneroOcean gulf.moneroocean.stream:443, SupportXMR pool.supportxmr.com:443, xmrpool.eu xmrpool.eu:443. Use --pool=tls://host:443 so the miner knows that port expects TLS. --connect-to with an address resolved somewhere else. SNI and Host stay intact; only the dial address changes. dig +short gulf.moneroocean.stream # from a network that resolves it zmrig -o gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 --connect-to 203.0.113.10:10001 -u 4YourMoneroAddress Option 4 is a workaround, not a solution: when the address changes, the connection breaks. Prefer 1–3. Details and the proxy recipes are in Networks that only allow 443.

documents.t: Country blocks. The client sees a refusal, not a reason. The cooldown stops it becoming a ban; it does not make that pool work. IPv6-only networks where the AAAA record is filtered — use --connect-to. Share rate limits (not login limits) on some pools. They arrive as rejects and the quarantine will stop the stream, but the right fix is fewer, larger shares via a higher target share time.
documents.s: What cannot be fixed from here

documents.t: Run one for a week, then the other, and compare xmrPerDay at the same hashrate: ./oneclick.sh install --pool=moneroocean --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress # a week later ./oneclick.sh install --pool=supportxmr --wallet 4YourMoneroAddress --failover=moneroocean --force MoneroOcean wins when the algorithm spread is real for your CPU (it changes with whichever coin is hot); SupportXMR wins when it is not, and always wins on steadiness. Measure, then decide — the answer changes from month to month.

Monero is the default because it has the deepest market and the only pool presets this repository can vouch for. It is not the only coin these engines can hash. zmrig hashes the whole RandomX family — rx/0, rx/wow, rx/arq, rx/graft, rx/sfx, rx/yada — plus Panthera, seven algorithms in all. That is the honest limit: a coin outside this list has no algorithm here, and no amount of configuration will make it mine one. All seven are covered by the test suite, one reference vector each, so "supported" means checked rather than advertised. Coin Ticker Algorithm Mine it with Monero XMR rx/0 --coin xmr (the default) Wownero WOW rx/wow --coin wow ArQmA ARQ rx/arq --coin arq Graft GRFT rx/graft --coin graft Safex Cash SFX rx/sfx --coin sfx YadaCoin YDA rx/yada --coin yada Scala XLA panthera --coin xla --coin is a shorter spelling of --algo rx/wow; both end up as the same "algo" in config.json. A name that is not in the table is refused with the list, before anything is written to the machine.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MoLik-Labs/ZMRIG/BETA/oneclick.sh \ | sudo bash -s -- install --wallet YOUR_ADDRESS --coin wow \ --pool pool.example.org:3333 --yes Look at the plan first — it prints the coin, the algorithm, the engine and the profile it resolved, and writes nothing: sudo ./oneclick.sh plan --wallet YOUR_ADDRESS --coin wow --pool pool.example.org:3333 engine zmrig (RandomX family, 1% dev fee) pool pool.example.org:3333 algo rx/wow coin Wownero profile free (auto: no battery, electricity is treated as free) The engine is chosen for you: rx/* and panthera are the Zig engine's territory (1 % of Monero time, --donate-level=0 to remove it). Force the C++ engine with --engine xmrig if you are debugging, not because it is faster — it is not.

The seven pool presets in the builder are Monero pools. Fees and endpoints for the smaller coins change too often for this repository to keep them accurate, so it does not carry them at all: --coin wow with no --pool is an error, not a guess. Get the endpoint from the coin's own community — usually a page or a pinned message in its chat — and pass it as host:port. If it publishes a separate TLS port, add --tls; if your network only allows 443, --cloudflare=host:port gives you WebSocket over TLS on the Zig engine.
documents.s: The endpoint is yours to supply

documents.t: The builder validates a Monero address exactly: 95 characters, 106 for an integrated address, base58 alphabet only. For the other six coins it checks the alphabet and a plausible length, and warns when the prefix is not the one it knows — it does not claim to validate a checksum it does not compute. The pool does that, and it is the only party that can. A wrong address mines for somebody else, and no page in a browser can prove an address is yours. Copy it from your own wallet, paste it, read the first and last six characters against the wallet screen.

documents.t: There is no fixed answer: it changes with the price, the network hashrate and your own hashrate. So the site does not print a recommendation built on numbers from last year. It computes one from numbers you supply. One rig, seven algorithms. Fill in a coin's own numbers and the table ranks what it actually pays per day — with your figures, not with mine. Fetch prices (CoinGecko)Forget my numbers Nothing is fetched until you press that button, so this page works offline and no request leaves your browser before you ask for one. A coin with a blank field shows why it cannot be ranked instead of a zero that looks like an answer, and no pool endpoint is invented for a coin this repository does not know. Reward, block time and network hashrate come from the coin's own explorer; prices from CoinGecko on request. The numbers stay in this browser. The arithmetic per coin: share = rig H/s ÷ network H/s blocks/day = 86400 ÷ block time coin/day = share × blocks/day × block reward $/day = coin/day × price Fill in reward, block time and network hashrate from the coin's explorer, and the price either by hand or with the CoinGecko button. A row with a blank field shows which field is missing instead of a zero — a zero would sort to the bottom and read like a real answer. Two things this table cannot see: Pool luck and fees. A small network's blocks are found rarely, so a rig at 0.1 % of it can wait days for a payout. That variance is real money on a one-machine setup, and none of it is in a daily average. Exchange depth. A coin's listed price means nothing if you cannot sell what you mine. Check that a market exists before pointing a rig at a coin that is new to you.

Nothing here is baked in at build time. Prices are fetched from CoinGecko only when you press the button, so the page works offline and no request leaves your browser before you ask. The figures you type stay in that browser. Re-check the numbers when the answer surprises you: a coin that leads by a factor of ten is usually a stale network hashrate, not a tenfold opportunity. Keeping the rig working Mining a different coin is a configuration change, not a different installer. If the coin's pool also pays for other algorithms, leave --coin off and let the pool pick: zmrig advertises the whole family at login, so the rig can move between them without a reinstall.

# a full run: 20 000 hashes, including the dataset build ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=20000 # a quick check after a configuration change ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 # the numbers for a dashboard (10 s warm-up + 15 s window) ./zmrig/out/zmrig --report --power 45 --bench uses the fixed seed 00112233…, a 76-byte blob and the lowest target, so every run hashes identical data and results are comparable. The dataset build (15–25 s) is outside the measured window. Rules that make a number mean something: Stop the miner before benchmarking. A running miner holds the huge pages; the bench then builds its dataset in ordinary memory and reports a figure that is too low. oneclick.sh bench stops and restarts the service to avoid this. Measure on the machine in question. Absolute hashrate depends on the host; do not compare to the table below. Run each configuration twice. Under 2 % is noise.

Configuration Hashrate vs default Comment Default: 2 threads, 1168 pages reserved, prefetch 1 800–841 H/s 100 % baseline, five runs No pages reserved, THP on (stock Ubuntu) 786 H/s 95 % what an unprivileged user gets No pages reserved, THP off 615–626 H/s 76 % the only case worth a root step --mode light 82 H/s 10 % only when RAM is short -t 1 408 H/s 50 % scales linearly -t 4 on two cores 798–801 H/s 98 % oversubscribing buys nothing --scratchpad-prefetch=0/2/3 1208–1302 kH/s (panthera) — inside the noise --no-affinity 814 H/s 100 % 2 vCPU, no difference The same machine and binary in a quieter session: 1008–1103 H/s. That spread is the reason comparisons have to be relative. C++ engine on the same machine, same session: 1075.7 H/s — the gap to the Zig engine is within run-to-run variance, not a performance claim.
documents.s: A 2 vCPU VM (Xeon 2.6 GHz, 1234 huge pages of 2 MiB)

documents.t: The largest and least ambiguous effect. RandomX reads a 2 GiB dataset in a random pattern, and 4 KiB pages mean constant TLB misses. # reserve 1168 pages of 2 MiB (≈2.3 GiB) — the size of rx/0, not of every coin echo 1168 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages grep HugePages_ /proc/meminfo The installer does this and writes it into the systemd unit (LimitMEMLOCK=infinity). The count follows the coin: panthera needs 96 pages (192 MB), not 1168. sudo zmrig-tune --algo panthera writes the right one, and zmrig sizes its own reservation the same way. To check the miner got them: startup logs huge pages … MB (explicit), and the API reports "hugepages": [granted, needed] — [1168, 1168] for rx/0, [96, 96] for panthera.

--no-huge-pages is not the same experiment as "the pages were never reserved". This miner passes MADV_HUGEPAGE on every mapping it makes, so on a kernel with transparent_hugepage=madvise (Ubuntu's default) an unprivileged run still gets 2 MiB pages, just not from the pool. The three states, rx/0, two runs each, same session: Pages Backing Hashrate 1168 reserved MAP_HUGETLB 814.5 / 832.2 H/s none reserved THP collapsed 99 % of the mapping 785.9 / 786.1 H/s none reserved, THP off 4 KiB 614.8 / 626.3 H/s So the step that matters is 4 KiB → 2 MiB (≈ +28 %), and the reserved pool is worth another 4–6 % on top. That is why the miner only asks for root when THP is off, and why startup prints the kernel's own count of collapsed pages (huge pages: 2332 MB via THP (99 % of the 2336 MB mapping, measured by the kernel)) instead of claiming the hint worked. A practical warning: with the full reservation in place, ordinary RAM is down to about 1.2 GB. Running --no-huge-pages at that point gets OOM-killed (exit 137), because the 2 GiB dataset has nowhere to live. Lower nr_hugepages to 0 first.

The 2 GiB dataset is a memory-bandwidth job, and it is the longest wait a rig has. Measured on this host, seed 00112233…: Initialiser threads dataset ready in 1 42.9 s 2 21.1 s --randomx-init=1 is therefore a way to make a seed change take twice as long; it is not a way to leave a core free for something else, because every core is waiting for the dataset anyway. The default is every hardware thread, even when mining is told to use fewer (-t 1 still builds with all of them).

fast builds one 2 GiB dataset shared by all threads → 849 H/s on this 2 vCPU machine. light keeps only the 256 MiB cache and recomputes the dataset per hash → 82 H/s. Nearly 10×. light is defensible when the VPS does not have the RAM, or to test a configuration quickly (0.6 s startup instead of 20 s).

Linear on this machine: 2 threads = 808–817 H/s, 1 thread = 408 H/s, 4 threads on two cores = 798–801 H/s. There is no hidden sweet spot and nothing above the core count. On a throttled shared vCPU, extra threads can lower per-thread hashrate while still raising the total; measuring is the only way to know.

--scratchpad-prefetch 0/1/2/3: under 1.5 %, i.e. noise. Leave the default. --no-affinity on 2 vCPU: nothing. --no-optimized-init: affects dataset build time, not hashrate. Ignore advice to raise priority for hashrate: priority changes how the OS shares CPU, it does not make arithmetic faster. It helps when the machine does other work.

documents.t: # 1. background state sudo ./oneclick.sh stop grep -E "HugePages_Total|HugePages_Free" /proc/meminfo # 2. measure the default ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 # 3. variants, each twice ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 -t 1 ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 --no-huge-pages # only after lowering nr_hugepages ./zmrig/out/zmrig --bench=15000 --mode light # 4. keep the winner in the config, then start sudo ./oneclick.sh start Write the numbers down with the date and host name. Six months later you will want them.

Hashrate is not the whole story. A machine doing 814 H/s at 95 W beats one doing 900 H/s at 130 W. Measure at the wall, or read package power from RAPL: cat /sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl:0/energy_uj # twice, one second apart zmrig --report reads it for you and records the source in the report code (pwsrc: rapl, hwmon, user or none), along with hw — hashes per watt (the 60-second hashrate divided by power). That is the number --profile watt optimises, so the code carries it instead of leaving everyone to divide. hashrate power H/W --profile free the most the machine can do highest lower --profile watt a few percent lower (SMT threads dropped) 30–40 % lower on the SMT part higher Those rows describe a direction, not your machine: power cannot be measured inside this repository's container (RAPL is blocked), so the watt figures are inferred from P ∝ V²·f and published SMT data. The hashrate side is measured. On a machine with RAPL, run zmrig --report under both profiles and compare hw — then the conclusion is yours, at your electricity price. The profitability calculator turns those watts into money.

zmrig mines 1 % of its Monero time for the developer. The other 99 % goes to the pool and wallet you configured. That is the whole policy: Rate 1 % of Monero (rx/0) mining time, --donate-level=0 to 10 Cadence 60 s of Monero mining to the developer wallet after every 100 minutes of yours Coin Monero only. The wallet is a Monero address, so ArQmA, Wownero, Graft, Safex, Yada and Scala time accrues nothing Destination the pool you already use, with the developer wallet in the login. No second pool, no relay, no hidden endpoint Switch --donate-level=0 or --no-donate turns it off completely Nothing is taken from a share you solved: a pool pays whoever logs in, so the only way a miner can pay a fee without sitting in the middle of your traffic is to log in with the other wallet for a while. The clock is debt-based, so a reconnect does not lose or double the fee: every second of Monero hashing adds 10 ms of debt at 1 % (100 ms at 10 %), once 60 s is owed, the miner ends the current connection and reconnects on the same pool with the developer wallet, to avoid a reconnect loop the cadence never exceeds one fee session per ~100 minutes at the default rate, and a pool that refuses the developer wallet postpones the fee by 2 minutes, then by 30 after three refusals, instead of interrupting your mining again.

It is not a silently applied setting. Every one of these says the rate and the address: ZMRIG 6.36.0 - RandomX miner by @nggkhaiz 1% of Monero mining time goes to the developer (--donate-level=0 turns it off), GPL-3.0, https://github.com/MoLik-Labs/ZMRIG zmrig ... --check | grep donate # donate 1% of Monero (rx/0) mining time to 46SQLW7DXaq6GJaQbHUFMAhd1VYpfQFJQ2gfZo9TCB8bf9vnf1MUwAD2Fwj6KMsY4RU3oKA3x6hByg8BKg7FfMWn6ysb5tJ, 60 s every 100 min (--donate-level=0 turns it off) At runtime, once per session: developer fee: 60 s owed, reconnecting to pay it developer fee: login ok, mining job 7f3a… for the developer wallet developer fee: session paid, back to your wallet And the HTTP API reports "donate_level": 1 in /1/summary and /2/summary, so a dashboard cannot show zero while the miner is paying.

Not a cut of your shares. Nothing is submitted twice, nothing is re-weighted, the pool never sees a share for a wallet you did not choose outside the fee window. Not payable in another coin. Mining ArQmA to a Monero address would burn the coins in a hole nobody can spend; the fee simply does not accrue there. Not a hardcoded pool. A fee session uses the pool, port, TLS and proxy settings of the pool you configured. If that pool does not accept the developer wallet, the fee is postponed and your mining is untouched.

./scripts/verify-fee.sh --binary zmrig/out/zmrig The script reads the fee constants, confirms --check prints the rate and the address, confirms --donate-level=0 prints off, and fails if a second donation host or a second wallet appears in the binary. Each check prints the line it read, so "it passed" is not the only output. zmrig ... --check | grep donate # the rate and the address zmrig ... --donate-level=0 # nothing is mined for anyone but you strings zmrig/out/zmrig | grep -c 46SQLW7D # exactly one address

src/ is the upstream XMRig tree with every donation line removed, and it still has no fee at all (doc/ZERO_FEE.md, ./scripts/verify-fee-free.sh). It is kept for algorithms the Zig engine does not speak and can be selected with --engine=xmrig; the default engine, zmrig, is the one that pays the fee. If you want to support the work, staying on the default engine is what does it.
documents.s: The C++ engine in this repo

documents.t: The same rate XMRig charges, for the same reason: it is small enough to be invisible in a profitability calculation (at 1 kH/s and any 2026 Monero price, 1 % of a month is worth less than the electricity of a single day) and large enough to fund the pool, the site and the testing that produced the numbers on these pages. It is time, not money: no invoice, no account, no tracking.

The Zig miner already takes 1 % of Monero time as a fee (what that costs); the C++ engine takes nothing. This page exists for the people who want to send something on top of that anyway. Nothing in the software reads the address below.

46SQLW7DXaq6GJaQbHUFMAhd1VYpfQFJQ2gfZo9TCB8bf9vnf1MUwAD2Fwj6KMsY4RU3oKA3x6hByg8BKg7FfMWn6ysb5tJ Monero (XMR) only. Anything else — BTC, ETH, USDT, wrapped tokens — is lost, and no one can recover it. A standard mainnet address, 95 characters, network byte 18. Not an integrated address, not a subaddress. The same wallet as the pool fee. pool/src/operator.js decodes to this exact address, and every pool instance publishes it at /api/config and on its status page. One wallet, one audit trail.

Do not trust a string because it is on GitHub. The address starts with 46SQLW7D and ends with n6ysb5tJ; a Monero address is base58 with a 4-byte Keccak-256 checksum, so a typo cannot survive a decode. from Crypto.Hash import keccak # pip install pycryptodome ALPHABET = "123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz" ADDRESS = "46SQLW7DXaq6GJaQbHUFMAhd1VYpfQFJQ2gfZo9TCB8bf9vnf1MUwAD2Fwj6KMsY4RU3oKA3x6hByg8BKg7FfMWn6ysb5tJ" def decode_block(text, size): value = 0 for char in text: value = value * 58 + ALPHABET.index(char) return value.to_bytes(size, "big") raw = b"" for offset in range(0, len(ADDRESS), 11): group = ADDRESS[offset:offset + 11] raw += decode_block(group, 8) if len(group) == 11 else decode_block(group, 5) body, checksum = raw[:-4], raw[-4:] digest = keccak.new(digest_bits=256, data=body).digest()[:4] print(len(raw), body[0], "OK" if digest == checksum else "BAD") # 69 18 OK A bad checksum means a typo, a truncated copy, or something that was never a Monero address.

No effect on the miner. Nothing parses this page at build or run time, and sudo ./oneclick.sh verify reports whichever fee the binary really takes, published address or not. No supporter edition. There is one binary and it mines at full speed for everybody. Anyone selling a "faster build" is not this project. No priority support, roadmap vote or badge. Issues are answered in the order they arrive and by how reproducible they are. No subscription. There is nothing recurring to cancel.
documents.s: What a donation does not buy

documents.t: Mine to the pool. The 1 % fee is what funds the work, and it only exists while somebody is mining. Send a measurement. zmrig/tests/ab.sh compares two settings on the same machine; a before/after table settles arguments that opinions do not. Report a bug with the command, the full output and the hardware. Light mode on a 2 GiB VPS and MSR reads on bare metal are where a report is worth the most. Send a patch. Pool share accounting, the Zig front end and doc/ typos are all fair game.
documents.s: What helps more than a transfer

documents.t: This project has published exactly one, the string above. Addresses in forks, issues, pull requests, videos, chat messages or "official mirror" sites are not ours. Compare against doc/DONATE.md in the repository history (git log -p doc/DONATE.md), not against a screenshot.

Donations are public on the Monero chain by design. Nothing else is collected: the miner sends no telemetry, the site has no analytics, and the pool keeps no account for a donor. To stay unlinked, send without a payment ID and from an address you have not used elsewhere.
